case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Parcel Logistics (MPL) is a partnership in the courier and parcel delivery sector, employing a workforce of 80 across its regional network. Founded in 2015 by Sofia Marchetti, the business sorts and delivers parcels for online retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. MPL plans to invest $540,000 in an automated parcel-sorting hub and electric delivery vans, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.50 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. Rising labour turnover and a growing parcel damage rate are increasing costs and harming MPL's service reputation.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — May 2025: MPL handled 42,000 parcels last month, with a damage rate of 2.7%, down from 3.9% the previous year. Lost parcels fell from 88 to 41 a month and average delivery time is 1.9 days. A survey of 500 online shoppers found that 73% rank delivery speed as the top priority and 58% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery. Staff records show 22 of 80 workers left in the past year; on-the-job training is provided at the depot, while off-the-job customer-service courses at the local college cost $650 per worker.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Parcel Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing interest on MPL's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.80 to $14.78 an hour, raising depot and courier wage costs. (3) Fuel and van-part input costs have risen 10.3% year-on-year, while transport inflation is 5.6% and online retail parcel volumes grew 4.8%.

questions.question_text: MPL has financed its sorting hub partly with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MPL of using retained profit for the $240,000 balance instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so using $240,000 of its own funds protects MPL's cash flow while it services the $300,000 five-year loan and meets fixed costs of $270,000 a year. The cash saved can instead cover the rising costs caused by 7.1% higher wages and 10.3% dearer fuel and van parts, protecting the $4.50 contribution earned on each of the 120,000 parcels without pushing the $9.00 price above what the 58% of shoppers willing to pay $1.50 more would accept.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids extra debt and keeps decision-making within the partnership. With no additional lender to satisfy, founders such as Sofia Marchetti can pursue the automated sorting hub at their own pace, which suits MPL's flat structure and laissez-faire style. It also avoids the collateral and arrangement fees that a larger loan would require, so the business is less exposed if the growing parcel damage rate delays efficiency gains. For a partnership where owners bear the risk, limiting borrowing is a prudent way to fund expansion during a period of rising labour turnover.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over extra borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MPL's expansion, financing and cost pressures.

questions.question_text: MPL wants to attract more online retailers. Consider local radio advertising, social media marketing, or sponsorship of a community event. Which should MPL choose to win new retailer contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can repeatedly reach listeners in MPL's regional network, carrying a simple message about 1.9-day delivery and the new electric vans. It suits a time-limited campaign around the $540,000 hub launch. However, reach is geographically narrow and mainly consumer-focused, while the purchasing decision lies with online retailers' logistics managers, so much of the spend would not influence contract awards.

Social media marketing: Targeted posts can showcase the automated sorter, the falling 2.7% damage rate and the $1.50 next-day option to a nationwide audience of retailers, with precise targeting and measurable clicks at low cost. Content must be sustained and conversion from a click to a formal contract can be slow, but results are trackable and the message can be updated quickly as the hub becomes operational.

Sponsorship of a community event: Sponsorship builds local goodwill and brand visibility, which may help with recruitment given that 22 of 80 workers left last year. It is indirect for winning retailer contracts, difficult to measure, and consumes funds that could improve the 1.9-day delivery record that 73% of shoppers prioritise.

Recommendation: MPL should choose social media marketing. It reaches the online retailers that matter, is affordable alongside the $300,000 loan, and can demonstrate the service improvements the 73% of 500 surveyed shoppers demand. Radio is rejected as too locally and consumer-focused for retailer procurement; community sponsorship is rejected because its link to contract winning is weak and it does nothing to address the damage rate or labour turnover that currently harm MPL's reputation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal reference to MPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to MPL and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in MPL's context with a clear recommendation explaining why radio and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: MPL's labour turnover is rising and its workforce of 80 works in a flat structure. Explain two benefits for MPL of using laissez-faire leadership.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives MPL's experienced couriers and depot staff freedom to organise their own routes and sorting routines, which suits a flat structure with few management layers. Autonomy can raise job satisfaction and help reduce the 22 of 80 workers who left last year, because employees who control their work are more likely to stay. Retaining experienced staff also protects service quality, helping to bring the 2.7% parcel damage rate down further and support the 1.9-day delivery time.

Point 2: Delegating decisions speeds up responses to local problems, which matters when lost parcels and delivery complaints must be handled quickly. With laissez-faire leadership, teams closest to the parcels can act on issues without waiting for approval, improving the reputation that 73% of surveyed shoppers link to delivery speed. It also frees managers to focus on the $540,000 sorting hub and electric vans. The style works best with skilled, motivated workers, so MPL should pair it with the $650 per-worker training to ensure staff can use their autonomy well.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MPL's turnover, structure and service data.

questions.question_text: MPL must reduce its 2.7% parcel damage rate and settle new starters. Consider on-the-job training at the depot or off-the-job customer-service courses at the local college. Which should MPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the depot directly covers MPL's own sorting equipment and handling methods, costs no fees, and keeps the 42,000 parcels handled each month moving while staff learn. Experienced workers can demonstrate correct loading techniques that reduce the 2.7% damage rate and the 41 lost parcels a month, and can pass on the habits that support 1.9-day delivery. The weaknesses are that trainers are working staff whose productivity falls, incorrect habits can spread, and there is no external certificate to reassure retailers.

Off-the-job courses: The local college charges $650 per worker, so training the 22 new or departing replacements would cost $14,300 (22 × $650), a modest sum against the $540,000 hub. Courses give structured customer-service skills and a recognised qualification, which can improve how staff deal with the complaints behind MPL's reputation problem. However, workers are away from the depot, temporarily slowing the 42,000-parcel throughput, and generic content may not address the specific causes of parcel damage in MPL's sorter.

Decision: MPL should choose on-the-job training first, supported by short college courses for new starters. On-the-job training is cheaper, tailored to the actual sorting hub and vans, and avoids losing throughput while labour turnover is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because $14,300 and time away from the depot would disrupt the 1.9-day service that 73% of shoppers prioritise, and it would not directly fix the 2.7% damage rate. Staggering the $650 courses for the 22 replacements would also limit the loss of throughput, and depot coaching would translate generic customer-service teaching into the specific handling routines that cut damage and the 41 lost parcels a month.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods with reference to MPL's costs and service record.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in MPL's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to damage.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($9.00 − $4.50) = $270,000 ÷ $4.50 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.00 − $4.50 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MPL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with 120,000 units actually handled gives a margin of safety of 60,000 units, confirming a strong buffer and supporting investment in the $540,000 sorting hub.
2. Contribution of $4.50 a unit lets managers assess the $1.50 next-day surcharge: if it added revenue without extra variable cost, contribution would rise to $6.00 and break-even would fall to $270,000 ÷ $6.00 = 45,000 units, showing the benefit of the 58% of shoppers who would pay more.
3. With fixed costs of $270,000, managers can set the parcel-volume target needed to service the $300,000 loan and check it against the 42,000 parcels handled each month while labour turnover persists.
4. Unit cost of $6.75 ($270,000 ÷ 120,000 units = $2.25 fixed cost per unit, plus $4.50 variable cost) can be benchmarked against the 10.3% fuel and van-part inflation, while labour productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 units per worker helps judge the impact of the 2.7% damage rate and staff departures.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 60,000 units vs 120,000 output; surcharge modelling vs $270,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume target; and unit-cost benchmarking at $6.75 with productivity of 1,500 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MPL's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MPL's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue of $3,200,000 in 2024 less cost of sales of $1,920,000 gives gross profit of $1,280,000; revenue of $3,600,000 in 2025 less $2,016,000 gives $1,584,000. Gross profit divided by revenue yields 40.0% and 44.0%. Operating profit of $480,000 in 2024 and $720,000 in 2025, each divided by revenue, yields 15.0% and 20.0%. Operating profit divided by capital employed of $2,400,000 and $2,880,000 yields 20.0% and 25.0%.

Evaluation: The picture is unambiguously positive. The first margin improved from 40.0% to 44.0%, showing MPL kept more of each revenue dollar after direct costs despite 7.1% higher wages and 10.3% dearer fuel and van parts, which is consistent with better control of the 120,000 units handled. The overall margin jumped from 15.0% to 20.0%, meaning overheads were absorbed far more effectively as revenue rose by $400,000. The return on capital climbed from 20.0% to 25.0%, so even though capital employed grew to $2,880,000, operating profit grew faster and the new sorting hub is already adding value. Interest payable fell from $60,000 to $55,000, giving further help with the $300,000 loan.

Conclusion: MPL's profitability has improved. All three ratios moved favourably at once, and the improvement is supported by rising revenue and gross profit rather than by accounting effects, while financing costs fell. The main caution is that the higher base rate and wage rise could reverse the trend if volumes weaken, so management should protect the 44.0% margin by cutting the 2.7% damage rate and the 22 departures that threaten service quality.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Correctly calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years with detailed evaluation of margins, capital use and financing costs and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MPL of offering guaranteed next-day delivery for $1.50 more.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $1.50 surcharge directly matches the 58% of 500 surveyed shoppers who said they would pay more for guaranteed next-day delivery, so it can raise revenue and protect the $4.50 contribution per unit as fuel and van-part costs rise 10.3%. It also gives MPL a clear service differentiator tied to the 1.9-day average delivery time and the new electric vans, helping win the online retailers that 73% of shoppers say prioritise speed.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing next-day delivery raises operating risk. If the growing parcel damage rate of 2.7% or the 22 staff departures cause missed promises, refunds and lost goodwill could outweigh the $1.50 gained, damaging the reputation the firm relies on. The insert gives no data on how many parcels would take the option or on extra delivery cost, so the net benefit cannot be quantified, and with fixed costs of $270,000 and a $300,000 loan, MPL has limited room to absorb any losses.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using MPL's survey, costs and service data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.3% rise in fuel and van-part costs will affect MPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If MPL's $300,000 loan is variable-rate, the additional interest is 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is small against fixed costs of $270,000 and the $240,000 retained profit already committed, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no increase. Higher rates could make future borrowing dearer and slightly slow online retail demand, but the direct cash effect is limited and can be managed by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.78 an hour): Depot and courier roles are largely hourly paid, so the rise lifts wage costs and matters because 22 of 80 staff already left. The insert provides no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage bill can be honestly invented; the defensible comparison is with given productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if turnover reduces output, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution per unit falls.

Input cost inflation (10.3% fuel and van parts): The $4.50 variable cost per unit is exposed to fuel and parts, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an explicit bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.3%, that would add 10.3% × $4.50 = $0.46 per unit, and at 120,000 units that is about $55,800 a year (120,000 × $0.46). Even a $0.30-per-unit rise would cost $36,000 a year. MPL can offset part of this through the $1.50 next-day surcharge accepted by 58% of shoppers.

Conclusion: The 10.3% rise in fuel and van-part costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 120,000 units and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that underpins the $540,000 investment. The interest rise is small and hedgeable, and the wage rise is significant but depends on unstated hours and on productivity MPL can influence, so neither matches the reach of input-cost inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to MPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on MPL's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
